key_terms.meaning: Fixing the relative positions of points on or near the earth and drawing them to scale on a map or plan
Surveying that treats the earth's surface as flat; used when the survey area is small enough that curvature error can be ignored
Surveying that accounts for the earth's curvature and uses a reference ellipsoid; used for large areas
Survey of land parcel boundaries for ownership records and land registration
Survey that fixes both horizontal position and elevation of natural and man-made features
How close a measured value is to the true value
How closely repeated measurements of the same quantity agree with each other
An error that follows a physical law or instrument defect, has the same sign and size under the same conditions, and can be corrected by a formula
Ratio of a map distance to the same horizontal ground distance, written 1:M (the RF)
A defined reference surface plus origin and orientation against which coordinates are computed
The equipotential surface of the earth's gravity field that best fits mean sea level, extended under the land
A mathematically smooth surface of revolution that approximates the geoid and is used for coordinate computation
Height of a point above the geoid, measured along the plumb line; the height shown by levelling
A permanently marked point of known reduced level to which all levelling in an area is referred
Distance of a point measured along the base line from the start point, usually in metres
A short measurement taken at right angles (or at a known angle) from a survey line to a detail point
Fixing intermediate points on a straight survey line between two end stations
Electronic distance measurement: distance found from the travel time or phase change of an electromagnetic wave sent to a target
Accuracy written as ±(a + b ppm × D), where a is a constant in mm, b is the scale error in parts per million and D is the measured distance in km
A small fixed correction added for the path inside the prism and the offset between instrument and prism vertical axes

takeaways: Surveying has one job: fix relative positions of points and draw them to scale, working from the whole to the part.
Plane surveying ignores curvature, geodetic surveying does not; the choice depends on the area and the accuracy needed.
Accuracy is closeness to truth, precision is repeatability; a set of readings can be precise and still wrong.
Gross errors are mistakes and are removed by re-measurement; systematic errors are corrected by formula; random errors are reduced by averaging.
Scale 1:M means one unit on the map equals M units on the ground, so a 1:1000 map is more detailed than a 1:25000 sheet.
Every coordinate needs a datum: an ellipsoid, a geoid, an origin and an orientation; heights above the geoid are orthometric heights and h = H + N.
Tape survey builds a skeleton of base, tie and check lines with offsets; tape corrections make the reading a true horizontal distance.
EDM replaces the chain; its accuracy is quoted as a fixed part plus a part proportional to distance, and atmospheric and prism corrections must be applied.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to state the principle of surveying, separate plane from geodetic, list and correct tape/EDM errors with formulas, and explain datum and coordinate concepts with a sketch.

bank.q: State the two basic principles of surveying and explain why surveying proceeds from the whole to the part.
outline: First principle: work from the whole to the part, fix a control framework of high accuracy first, then fill in detail.
Second principle: fix a point by at least two independent measurements (two distances, two angles, or distance and bearing).
Prevents accumulation of errors, keeps detail consistent with control, allows checks at every stage.
Example: control traverse first, then offsets from it.
answer: What surveying must achieve. Surveying fixes the relative positions of points and draws them to scale. Two working rules make this possible with ordinary instruments: work from the whole to the part, and fix every new point by at least two independent measurements from points already fixed.

First principle: whole to part. First fix a few widely spaced control stations with the best method and the most care (a closed traverse, a triangulation net or GNSS), and check that the frame closes. Then fix secondary stations from the frame, and only then pick up detail (buildings, fences, trees) from the nearest stations by short offsets or short radial shots.

answer.text: Why the order matters: errors stay local. Suppose a 2 km boundary is built from twenty 100 m lines laid one after another, each with a random error of ±0.02 m. The errors add in quadrature, so the far end is uncertain by about √20 × 0.02 m, and every bearing error swings the line further. Worked from a control frame, each short line is held between two fixed points and its error cannot travel past them.
answer.pre:
part to whole:  end error ≈ √n × e = √20 × 0.02 = 0.089 m (and growing with every extra line)
whole to part:  error of a detail point ≈ error of one short line ≈ 0.02 m

answer: The frame also gives checks. A closed traverse must close; a check line measured across a chain-survey triangle must agree with the plotted length. A detail survey that starts from the parts has nothing to close on, so a blunder spreads unseen through everything that follows.

answer.text: Second principle: two independent measurements. From two fixed points A and B, a new point P can be fixed by two distances (trilateration, chain triangles), a chainage and a perpendicular offset, two angles (intersection), an angle and a distance (radiation, as a total station does), or two oblique offsets (tie measurements). Worked case: A and B are 50 m apart, AP = 30 m and BP = 40 m.
answer.pre:
distance of the foot of P along AB:  x = (AB² + AP² − BP²) / (2 AB)
                                    = (2500 + 900 − 1600) / 100 = 18.0 m
offset of P from AB:                 y = √(AP² − x²) = √(900 − 324) = 24.0 m

answer: Two candidates. Two circles meet at two points, so P can lie 24.0 m to the left or to the right of AB. The field sketch, or a third measurement (a check line), decides which. A single measurement only puts P somewhere on a circle or a line, so it never fixes a point.

How the two principles work together. The frame comes first (principle one), and each frame station and each detail point is fixed by two measurements from points already fixed (principle two). A highway survey shows both: GNSS control points every few kilometres, a traverse between them, then offsets to the road edges and trees from the traverse lines.
Check. In the worked case 18² + 24² = 324 + 576 = 900 = 30², and (50 − 18)² + 24² = 1024 + 576 = 1600 = 40², so P satisfies both measured distances.

bank.q: Classify surveys by purpose, by instrument used and by the treatment of the earth's curvature, giving one use for each type.
outline: By purpose: topographic, cadastral, engineering, control, hydrographic, astronomical.
By instrument: chain/tape, compass, theodolite, total station, GNSS.
By curvature: plane surveying (small areas, flat earth) versus geodetic surveying (large areas, ellipsoid).
One practical use for each class, stated in one line.
answer: Why classify. The class of a survey tells the party what to measure, which instrument to carry and how precise the work must be. Three common bases are used: the purpose, the instrument, and whether the curvature of the earth is taken into account.

answer.text: By purpose.

head: Class
What it fixes
One use
rows: natural and built features and the relief of the ground
boundaries, ownership and areas of land parcels
design data and setting out of works
pegging out a bridge or pipeline
an accurate frame of reference points
the frame for every other survey of a city
depths, shore lines and the bed of water bodies
latitude, longitude and azimuth from stars or the sun
checking the azimuth of older control

answer.text: By instrument.

head: Class
What it measures
One use
rows: a house plot or small level site
a rough traverse in open country
angles and distances, coordinates in the field
detail and setting out on a building site

answer: By the treatment of curvature. Plane surveying treats the earth as flat; it is used for areas up to about 250 km² and ordinary sights, such as a town or a canal reach. Geodetic surveying works on the spheroid; it is used for national control, long baselines and large areas.

answer.text: Size of the curvature effect. The departure of a level line from a horizontal line over a sight d is c = d²/(2R), with R = 6371 km.

answer: Other bases. Surveys are also named by where they are done (land, hydrographic, underground, aerial) and by method (triangulation, traversing, levelling). These overlap with the three bases above.

One project, several classes. A 40 km highway starts with a control survey (GNSS points), uses a topographic survey to choose the alignment, a cadastral survey to acquire the land and an engineering survey to set out the centre line. It is geodetic in its control and plane in its detail.

answer.text: Curvature in angles as well. On a curved surface the angles of a triangle add to more than 180° by the spherical excess ε = A/R² radians. One second of excess needs an area of 4.848 × 10⁻⁶ × 6371² = 197 km²:
answer.pre:
ε = 1″  when  A = 4.848 × 10⁻⁶ rad × (6371 km)² = 197 km²
so triangles of ordinary plane surveys (a few km²) have an excess far below 1″

answer: Choosing the class in practice. Ask three questions: what must the result show (purpose), what precision and what kind of measurement does that need (instrument), and how large is the area (plane or geodetic). The answers fix the class, and the class fixes the specification, the party and the cost.
Check. Each class above is defined by what it measures or fixes, and each has one use. The curvature figures follow from c = d²/(2R): for 5 km, 5000²/(2 × 6 371 000) = 25 000 000/12 742 000 = 1.96 m.

bank.q: Distinguish between accuracy and precision, and between gross, systematic and random errors, with one example of each.
outline: Definitions of accuracy and precision; the four combinations of high/low.
Gross error: observer mistake, wrong booking, wrong reading; detected by repeats.
Systematic error: tape too long, temperature, refraction; same sign and magnitude, corrected by formula.
Random error: pointing and reading, small and both signs, reduced by averaging, follows a error curve.
answer: Definitions. Accuracy is how close a result (one reading, or the mean of a set) is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated readings are to one another. Accuracy is about bias; precision is about scatter.

answer.text: Worked case. A line of true length 100.00 m is taped five times: 100.02, 100.04, 100.03, 100.05 and 100.01 m.

answer: Verdict on the set. The scatter (s = 0.016 m) is small, so the set is precise. The mean is 0.03 m high, about four times its own uncertainty of 0.007 m, so the set is not accurate: a systematic error is present.

The four combinations. Accurate and precise is the goal. Precise but not accurate (as above) calls for calibration and a correction. Accurate but not precise calls for more readings and a mean. Neither calls for the work to be redone.

answer.text: The three kinds of error.

head: Kind
Cause
Sign and size
Effect of averaging
Remedy
Example
rows: 24.60 booked as 26.40, an error of 1.80 m
instrument, observer or nature, under a fixed law
same sign and size each time
a 30 m tape 8 mm too long reads 300 m as 299.92 m

answer: Numbers in the examples. The 8 mm tape over 300 m: 300/30 = 10 tape lengths, each reading 8 mm short, so 10 × 0.008 = 0.08 m short, whatever the number of repeats. The blunder of 1.80 m is found by a check line or by measuring the line in the other direction.

How the scatter is read. For random errors about two readings in three fall within ±s of the mean and about 95 % within ±2s. Here ±2s = ±0.032 m, so a sixth reading of 100.10 m (0.07 m from the mean, more than 4s) would be suspected as a blunder and checked.

answer.text: How the two kinds grow along a line. Over n tape lengths a systematic error adds directly (n × e), a random error only as √n × e. For 10 lengths with a systematic 8 mm and a random ±3 mm per length:
answer.pre:
systematic: 10 × 8 mm = 80 mm
random:     √10 × 3 mm = 9.5 mm

answer.text: Sources of systematic error.

head: Source
Example
Correction
rows: tape not of standard length; EDM prism constant wrong
compare with a standard, apply the constant
an observer who always reads a vernier slightly high
measure the conditions and correct by formula

answer: Closing check. In the worked case, the deviations add to zero (−0.01 + 0.01 + 0 + 0.02 − 0.02 = 0), as they must about a mean, and the correction to apply is −0.03 m once the cause (here a short tape) is confirmed on a standard baseline.

bank.q: Explain what a datum is. Describe the geoid, the reference ellipsoid and the relation between ellipsoidal height, orthometric height and geoid undulation.
outline: Datum = reference surface + origin + orientation + (for modern datums) an ellipsoid.
Geoid: mean sea level surface extended under land; ellipsoid: mathematical approximation.
h = H + N, define each symbol and its units.
Why a coordinate without a datum is meaningless; mention WGS84 as a geocentric datum.
answer: Datum. A datum is the reference against which positions and heights are given: a reference surface, its size and shape, and how it is placed and oriented on the earth (origin and axes). A horizontal datum carries latitude and longitude; a vertical datum carries heights.

Geoid. The geoid is the equipotential surface of the earth's gravity that best fits mean sea level, continued under the land. Water does not flow along it, and a levelling instrument's bubble is set perpendicular to it. It is uneven, rising and falling by tens of metres because the mass inside the earth is uneven.

Reference ellipsoid. An ellipsoid of revolution, defined by its semi-major axis a and flattening f, is smooth enough for formulas. WGS84, the datum of GPS, uses a = 6 378 137 m and f = 1/298.257 223 563. A local datum such as the older Indian datum fits an ellipsoid (Everest) closely to one region instead of to the whole earth.

answer.text: Three heights. h, the ellipsoidal height, is measured from the ellipsoid along its normal (what GNSS gives). H, the orthometric height, is measured from the geoid along the plumb line (what levelling gives). N, the geoid undulation, is the height of the geoid above the ellipsoid. They are related by h = H + N, so H = h − N, all in metres.

answer.text: Worked case. A GNSS receiver gives h = 52.3 m where a geoid model gives N = −82.0 m. A second point has h = 100.0 m and N = +30.0 m.
answer.pre:
point 1:  H = h − N = 52.3 − (−82.0) = 134.3 m   (geoid below the ellipsoid: H > h)
point 2:  H = h − N = 100.0 − 30.0  = 70.0 m    (geoid above the ellipsoid: H < h)

answer: Why a coordinate needs its datum. The same pillar has different latitude and longitude on WGS84 and on a local datum, and different heights above the ellipsoid and above the geoid. Coordinates from two datums are transformed to one before they are combined; heights from GNSS are turned into levelled heights with a geoid model.

answer.text: The ellipsoid in numbers. From a and f the semi-minor axis and the eccentricity follow:
answer.pre:
b = a (1 − f) = 6 378 137 × (1 − 1/298.257 223 563) = 6 356 752.3 m
e² = 2f − f² = 0.006 694 38
so the polar radius is 21.4 km shorter than the equatorial radius

answer: Vertical datum. Orthometric heights start from mean sea level found from years of tide gauge records and carried inland by precise levelling to a network of benchmarks. A height quoted "above mean sea level" refers to that datum; a GNSS height above the ellipsoid does not, until N is subtracted.

answer.text: Height differences over a site. Over a few kilometres N changes slowly, so GNSS height differences are almost levelled differences, but not quite. Two points 2 km apart:
answer.pre:
point A: h = 52.3 m, N = −82.0 m → H = 134.3 m
point B: h = 54.1 m, N = −82.3 m → H = 136.4 m
Δh = 1.8 m, but ΔH = 2.1 m: ignoring the 0.3 m change in N gives a 0.3 m error in the rise

answer: Check. Substitute back: H + N = 134.3 + (−82.0) = 52.3 m = h, and 70.0 + 30.0 = 100.0 m = h. The relation holds for both signs of N.

bank.q: Define scale. Distinguish a large-scale map from a small-scale map, and list the marginal information found on a topographic sheet.
outline: Scale = map distance / ground distance = 1:M.
1:1000 is a larger scale than 1:50000; large scale shows more detail over a smaller area.
Marginal information: sheet number and name, scale, contour interval, north direction, legend, benchmark values, adjoining sheet index.
Plain statement of the representative fraction and graphic scale.
answer: Scale. Scale is the ratio of a distance on the map to the same horizontal distance on the ground. Written as a representative fraction, RF = 1/M, it has no unit because both lengths are in the same unit. A statement such as "1 cm = 250 m" is the same scale as RF = 1/25 000, since 250 m = 25 000 cm.

answer.text: Large and small scale. A scale is larger when the fraction is larger, that is when M is smaller. A large scale shows a small area in detail; a small scale shows a large area with little detail.
Using the scale. On a 1:50 000 sheet two points 7.2 cm apart are 7.2 × 50 000 = 360 000 cm = 3.6 km apart. A plain scale to read 5 km on the same sheet is 5 × 100 000/50 000 = 10 cm long.
answer.pre:
ground = map × M        7.2 cm × 50 000 = 360 000 cm = 3.6 km
bar     = ground / M    500 000 cm / 50 000 = 10 cm

answer: Graphical scale. The sheet also carries a drawn bar. If the map is copied larger or smaller, the printed RF becomes wrong, but the bar changes with the drawing and stays true. Diagonal and vernier scales read finer than a plain bar.

Marginal information on a topographic sheet. The sheet name and number in the national index, with the numbers of the adjoining sheets; the RF and a drawn scale; the contour interval; the grid and its ticks; the north diagram with true, grid and magnetic north and the magnetic declination for the year; the legend of conventional signs; the year of survey and of edition; and the datum and projection to which positions and spot heights refer.

Why each item matters. The scale converts lengths; the contour interval converts the spacing of contours into slope; the north diagram lets a compass be used with the sheet; the datum tells a GNSS user whether coordinates can be compared directly.

answer.text: A shrunk sheet. If the 10 cm bar on an old 1:50 000 sheet now measures 9.8 cm, the sheet has shrunk by the factor 0.98:

answer: Check. 1:1 000 against 1:50 000: 1/1 000 = 0.001 is larger than 1/50 000 = 0.000 02, so 1:1 000 is the larger scale, as the table shows (the plot is 2 cm long, not 0.4 mm).

bank.q: A 30 m steel tape is standard at 20 °C and 100 N, with cross-section 3 mm², weight 0.25 N/m, E = 2.0 × 10⁵ N/mm² and α = 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ per °C. It is used at 32 °C with a pull of 150 N, supported only at its ends, to measure one full bay on a slope whose ends differ in level by 1.5 m. Explain each correction, give its formula and sign, and find the true horizontal length of the bay.
outline: Standardisation: C = (L′ − L) M / L; zero here, the tape is standard
Temperature: C = M α (T − T₀), positive when hotter
Tension: C = (P − P₀) M / (A E), positive when the pull exceeds the standard
Sag: C = −w² l³/(24 P²), always negative
Slope: C = √(M² − h²) − M, always negative; alignment works the same way
Sum the corrections with their signs and add to the measured length
answer: Sign convention. Each correction C is added to the measured length M to give the true length: true = M + C. A tape that reads too little needs a positive correction.
Standardisation. C = (L′ − L) M / L, where L′ is the actual length of the tape and L its nominal length. The tape is standard at 20 °C and 100 N, so L′ = L and C = 0 here.
Temperature. C = M α (T − T₀). A hot tape is longer than its marks say, so it reads too little and C is positive: 30 × 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ × (32 − 20) = +0.004 03 m.

Tension (pull). C = (P − P₀) M / (A E). A harder pull stretches the tape, so it reads too little and C is positive: (150 − 100) × 30 / (3 × 2.0 × 10⁵) = 1500/600 000 = +0.002 50 m. Units: N, m, mm² and N/mm², so the mm² cancel.

Sag. C = −w² l³/(24 P²) for one span. A sagging tape bows below the straight line, so the chord is shorter than the reading and C is always negative: −(0.25² × 30³)/(24 × 150²) = −1687.5/540 000 = −0.003 13 m.

Slope. C = √(M² − h²) − M. The tape lies along the slope, which is longer than its horizontal projection, so C is always negative: √(30² − 1.5²) − 30 = √897.75 − 30 = 29.962 48 − 30 = −0.037 52 m. Alignment (the tape held off the line by a distance d) uses the same form with d in place of h.

answer.text: Total.

answer: True horizontal length. 30.000 − 0.034 12 = 29.966 m. The slope term is ten times larger than the others; the temperature and tension terms happen to nearly cancel the sag.

Order of size. Slope −37.5 mm, temperature +4.0 mm, sag −3.1 mm, tension +2.5 mm. Over a 600 m line of twenty such bays the total would be 20 × −0.034 12 = −0.682 m, a relative error of 1 in 880 if the corrections were ignored, far worse than careful taping at 1 in 5000.

answer.text: Slope by the short formula. For small h the slope correction is about −h²/(2l):
Normal tension. The pull at which tension and sag corrections cancel satisfies (P − P₀) l/(AE) = w² l³/(24 P²). With W = wl = 7.5 N and AE = 6.0 × 10⁵ N, solving by trial:

answer: Field practice. Read the temperature at the tape, not in the shade; apply the pull with a spring balance; support the tape at its ends only when that is how it was standardised, or use the catenary formula; and for the slope, either measure h by levelling or the slope angle θ and use M(cos θ − 1).

Check. At 150 N the sag correction is (100/150)² = 0.444 of its value at the standard pull of 100 N (−0.007 03 m), and 0.444 × 0.007 03 = 0.003 12 m, agreeing with the direct result. The pull that makes sag and tension cancel exactly is the normal tension, a little above 150 N here.

bank.q: An EDM gives an accuracy of plus or minus (3 mm + 3 ppm). Compute the expected error for distances of 100 m, 1 km and 5 km and comment on which term dominates.
outline: Formula: error = a + b times D in km.
Constant term dominates at short range, ppm term at long range.
State that atmospheric correction and prism constant must also be applied.
answer: The specification. ±(3 mm + 3 ppm) means a constant part a = 3 mm on every distance, plus a part that grows with distance, b = 3 ppm = 3 mm per km. The expected error is σ = a + b × D with D in km.

answer.text: Computed errors.

answer: Which term dominates. At 100 m the constant part is 3/3.3 = 91 % of the error; the two parts are equal at D = a/b = 3/3 = 1 km; at 5 km the ppm part is 15/18 = 83 %. Short lines are limited by the constant (zero error, prism constant, centring), long lines by the ppm part (atmosphere and frequency).

Relative accuracy improves with length. Dividing the distance by the error: 100/0.0033 = 30 300 and 5000/0.018 = 277 800. A short line is relatively the weakest, so short legs in a traverse deserve extra care in centring.

What the figure does not include. The specification assumes the prism constant and the atmospheric correction are right. A wrong prism constant adds its full error to every line; a temperature wrong by 10 °C changes the distance by about 10 ppm, more than three times the ppm part here.
Practice. Enter the prism constant for the prism in use, measure temperature and pressure at the instrument, measure each line in both directions, and check the instrument on a calibrated baseline.

Where the two parts come from. The constant part comes from the zero error and prism constant, the phase-measurement resolution and the centring of instrument and prism; it is the same on any length. The ppm part comes from the uncertainty of the modulation frequency and of the refractive index of the air (temperature, pressure, humidity), which scales every distance.

answer.text: Root-sum-square form. Some makers combine the parts as √(a² + (bD)²), which gives a slightly smaller figure:
answer.pre:
1 km:  √(3² + 3²)  = √18  = 4.2 mm   (against 6 mm by simple addition)
5 km:  √(3² + 15²) = √234 = 15.3 mm  (against 18 mm)

answer.text: A short leg. On a 50 m traverse leg the error is 3 + 3 × 0.05 = 3.15 mm, a relative accuracy of 50/0.003 15 = 1 in 15 900. That is still better than careful taping at 1 in 5000, but much weaker than the same instrument on a long line.

answer: Check. At 1 km both parts are 3 mm, so the total is twice the constant: 6 mm, as in the table.

bank.q: Describe the field procedure for a chain and tape survey of a small plot: ranging, base line, tie lines, check lines and offsets, and how the plot is drawn afterwards.
outline: Reconnaissance and sketch of the area, fix stations so lines are unobstructed.
Direct ranging by eye and by line ranger between stations; indirect ranging when ends are not intervisible.
Measure base line and all tie and check lines; book in a field book with a neat diagram.
Take perpendicular and oblique offsets with a cross staff or optical square, note chainage and offset in metres.
Check: the check line computed from the plotted triangle must agree with the measured value.
Plot to scale, fit offsets, compare with the check line, correct closing error if any.
answer: Equipment. A 20 m or 30 m chain or a steel tape, ranging rods, ten arrows, a cross-staff or optical square, pegs, a field book and pencil.

Reconnaissance and index sketch. Walk the plot; choose stations so that the lines form well-shaped triangles (no angle below about 30°), the lines are on clear ground, and every feature is near a line. Draw an index sketch of the stations and lines.

answer.text: Worked plot. Stations A, B, C, D. Base line AC = 120 m through the middle; triangle ABC on one side with AB = 70 m and BC = 80 m; triangle ACD on the other with AD = 60 m and CD = 90 m; BD is the check line.

answer: Ranging and chaining. Range each line directly where its ends are visible, or by reciprocal ranging over a rise. Chain from A towards C, the follower holding the zero end and the leader putting an arrow at each chain length; ten arrows passed back record 10 chain lengths. On sloping ground hold the tape horizontal and step down, or measure along the slope and apply the slope correction.

answer.text: Offsets and booking. At each feature near AC, find the foot of the perpendicular with the cross-staff and book the chainage and the offset. The field book is filled from the bottom of the page upwards.
The check line. Before leaving the site, compute BD from the triangle sides and compare it with the measured BD.

answer: Plotting. At 1:500 the base line is 120 m/500 = 24 cm. Plot AC, swing arcs of 70 and 80 m (14 and 16 cm) from A and C to fix B, and of 60 and 90 m to fix D; then plot each offset at its chainage. Measure BD on the plan: it should be 89.29/500 = 17.9 cm. A field BD within the allowed error confirms the frame; a larger difference means a line is re-measured, never that offsets are stretched to fit.

answer.text: Are the triangles well conditioned? The angles from the cosine rule:

answer: Check lines and tie lines. A check line (BD here) runs between two stations of the frame, or from a station to a point on an opposite line, only to test the frame. A tie line joins two points on main lines to carry a subsidiary line close to detail that is too far for offsets, such as a pond in the middle of the plot.

Obstacles. Over a rise that hides one end from the other, range by reciprocal ranging from two intermediate points. Past a pond, set out equal perpendiculars at two chainages on either side and chain the parallel line between their feet, which is equal to the hidden length. Past a building, a parallel line by perpendicular offsets does the same.

Allowed mismatch on the check line. At an ordinary 1 in 500, BD may differ from 89.29 m by 89.29/500 = 0.18 m. A measured BD of 89.20 m (0.09 m short) passes; 88.70 m (0.59 m short) fails and the frame lines are re-measured.
Check. The area of ABCD from the frame is ½ × 120 × (44.84 + 43.57) = 5305 m², a useful second check against the plotted plan.

bank.q: A tape 30 m long is found to be 0.02 m too short. It measures a line as 1200 m at a temperature of 35 degrees C when standardised at 20 degrees C. Apply the standardisation and temperature corrections and state the true distance.
outline: Standardisation: a short tape over-reads, so the correction is negative: −(0.02/30) × 1200 m
Temperature: C = 1200 × 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ × (35 − 20), positive
Combine the two corrections with their signs
State the true distance to two decimals; sag and slope are not given, so not applied
answer: Convention. True length = measured length + corrections. A tape that is too short lays out less than 30 m for every "30 m" it counts, so it over-reads and its correction is negative. A tape used hotter than its standard temperature is longer, so it under-reads and its correction is positive.

answer.text: Standardisation correction. The tape is 0.02 m short in 30 m, so the correction is −0.02 m for every 30 m measured.

answer: The same by counting. 1200/30 = 40 tape lengths, each 0.02 m short: 40 × 0.02 = 0.80 m too much was read.

answer.text: Temperature correction.
Combined.

answer: Result. The true distance is 1199.40 m. The two corrections act in opposite directions: the short tape makes the reading too large, the heat makes the tape longer and the reading smaller.
What is not applied. No pull, sag or slope data is given, so those corrections are left out; if the line were on a slope or measured in suspended bays they would be added the same way.

answer.text: Measuring and setting out are opposite.

head: Tape
Measuring a line
Setting out a given length
rows: lays out too little: add tape lengths
lays out too much: take tape lengths off

answer.text: Setting out with the same tape. To set out a true 1200 m at 35 °C with this tape, each tape length really covers 29.985 04 m, so the reading to lay out is larger:
Areas with a wrong tape. Every length is wrong by the same factor, so an area is wrong by the factor squared. A plot found to be 4.00 ha with the short tape at its standard temperature is really

answer: Size of the net correction. −0.800 + 0.2016 = −0.5984 m in 1200 m is 1 in 2005. Left out, it would be a systematic error of 0.6 m that no amount of repetition would show.

The value of α. 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ per °C is the usual figure for a steel tape (11 to 12 × 10⁻⁶); an invar tape has about one thirtieth of it and is used on base lines where temperature cannot be measured well.

Check. Work it the other way: the tape's real length at 35 °C is (30 − 0.02) × (1 + 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ × 15) = 29.98 × 1.000168 = 29.985 04 m. Forty such lengths are 40 × 29.985 04 = 1199.40 m, the same answer.

bank.q: Compare chain and tape surveying with EDM and total station work for a topographic survey of a 5 hectare site. Judge which you would choose and justify.
outline: Chain and tape: cheap, no power, accurate for short distances, slow, limited by ground and obstructions, errors accumulate with many offsets.
EDM and total station: measures slope distance and angles, reduces to coordinates in the field, longer range, needs calibration and atmospheric correction.
Compare initial cost, speed, accuracy per point, manpower, data handling.
Justify a choice with the site size, terrain and required accuracy; note that a control framework is needed either way.
Mention GNSS as the control option.
answer: The site. 5 hectares is 50 000 m², for example 250 m × 200 m. Its perimeter is 2 × (250 + 200) = 900 m and its diagonal √(250² + 200²) = 320.2 m.

Chain and tape. A 30 m tape covers the perimeter in 900/30 = 30 tape lengths and the diagonal in 11. It needs no power and little money, and it is accurate on short level lines. It cannot measure angles, so detail is fixed by offsets from lines, and every building, hedge or slope across a line is an obstacle. The errors are systematic per tape length (temperature, pull, sag, slope) and must be corrected line by line.
Accuracy on the diagonal. Careful steel taping at 1 in 5000 gives 320.2/5000 = 0.064 m on the 320 m diagonal. An EDM of ±(3 mm + 3 ppm) gives 3 + 3 × 0.320 = 4.0 mm on the same line.

EDM and total station. One set-up near the middle reaches every corner (the farthest is about 160 m away), measures angle and slope distance together and stores coordinates directly. Obstacles matter only if they block the line of sight. It needs calibration, batteries, the atmospheric and prism corrections, and a trained observer.

answer.text: Comparison.

answer: Judgement. For a topographic survey, which needs both position and height of many points, the total station is the better choice: it gives about sixteen times better accuracy on the long line and heights without a separate levelling. Chain and tape remains sensible for a small, level, open plot where only a boundary plan is wanted, or as a check on a few total station distances.
Control in either case. Both methods need a frame: a few stations fixed and checked first. GNSS can fix two or three of them on the national datum so the plan can be joined to other maps.

Heights. A topographic survey needs heights. With chain and tape they come from a separate levelling on a grid: a 25 m grid over 250 m × 200 m has (250/25 + 1) × (200/25 + 1) = 11 × 9 = 99 points, each a staff reading. A total station gives the height of every detail point with its position, from the vertical angle and slope distance.

answer.text: Height from one total station shot. Instrument height 1.50 m on a station of reduced level 20.000 m; slope distance 120.000 m at a vertical angle of +2°00′; prism height 1.80 m:

answer: Risks of each. Chain and tape: slope and temperature corrections forgotten, a tape length dropped from the count, offsets too long. Total station: wrong prism constant or atmospheric setting, a flat battery, a wrong station or backsight entered, so that hundreds of points are wrong together; always re-observe a known point at the end.

A mixed plan for the 5 ha site. Two or three GNSS control points, a short total station traverse round them, total station detail and heights, and a few tape checks between hard detail such as building corners.
Check. 64 mm/4.0 mm = 16, the factor quoted; and 250 × 200 = 50 000 m² = 5 ha, the area given.

bank.q: A student claims that averaging many readings removes all error. Evaluate this claim using the ideas of gross, systematic and random errors.
outline: Averaging reduces only random errors, roughly by 1 over square root of n.
Systematic errors survive averaging; they shift the mean and need a formula or calibration.
Gross errors distort the mean badly; they must be found and removed first.
Conclusion: accuracy needs correction plus averaging, not averaging alone.
Give a tape example: a tape 0.05 m too long stays wrong however many times it is used.
answer: The claim. "Averaging many readings removes all error." It is true only for one of the three kinds of error.

answer.text: Random errors are reduced. If one reading scatters with s = 0.02 m, the mean of n readings scatters with s/√n.
answer.pre:
n = 4:   0.02/√4  = 0.010 m
n = 16:  0.02/√16 = 0.005 m   (four times the readings, half the error)

answer.text: Systematic errors survive. A 30 m tape that is 0.05 m too long reads a true 300 m line as 300 × 30/30.05 = 299.50 m every time. Averaging a hundred such readings still gives 299.50 m.
answer.pre:
each reading:  300 × 30 / 30.05 = 299.50 m
mean of any number of readings: 299.50 m   (error −0.50 m stays)

answer.text: Gross errors corrupt the mean. Five readings: 299.51, 299.49, 299.50, 299.52 and 329.50 m (a whole tape length dropped from the count in the last).

answer: So the correct order is: find and remove blunders by checks (the 329.50 m reading is 30 m from the rest); remove systematic errors by calibration and correction (here, the tape correction of +0.50 m found by comparing the tape on a standard baseline); then average what is left to reduce random error.
Verdict. The claim is false. Averaging improves precision, not accuracy. A precise mean can still be wrong by the whole systematic error, and one blunder can move it by metres.

Why random errors cancel. Random errors are equally likely to be positive or negative and small ones are more common than large ones, so in a sum they partly cancel. Their total grows only as √n while the sum of the readings grows as n, so the error of the mean falls as 1/√n.

answer.text: Spotting the blunder by the scatter. The four good readings have mean 299.505 m and s = 0.013 m. The fifth is 30 m away, more than two thousand times s:

answer: Surveying errors that averaging leaves alone. Tape temperature and sag; a wrong EDM prism constant; collimation error of a level (removed by equal back and fore sight lengths, not by repetition); local attraction on a compass. Each has the same sign every time, so each needs a correction or a field method that cancels it.

Diminishing returns. Going from 16 to 64 readings halves the random error again, from 0.005 m to 0.0025 m, at four times the work; past a point the systematic error left over is larger than the random part, and more readings buy nothing.
Check. Corrected result: 299.505 + 0.50 = 300.005 m, within the 0.005 m random uncertainty of the true 300 m.

bank.q: Explain why a latitude and longitude pair without a stated datum, and a height without a stated reference surface, are of limited use in engineering work.
outline: Same physical point gets different coordinates on different datums; shifts can be tens to hundreds of metres.
Datum transformation converts coordinates between datums; parameters must be stated.
Height may be ellipsoidal (GNSS) or orthometric (levelling); they differ by the geoid undulation N.
Engineering uses: setting out, GIS overlay, flood levels; a wrong datum gives a wrong position or level.
Recommend recording datum, epoch and projection with every coordinate set.
answer: A coordinate is a measurement from a reference. Latitude is the angle between the ellipsoid normal and the equatorial plane; longitude is the angle from the prime meridian; both are defined only on a stated ellipsoid placed in a stated way, that is, on a datum.

Different datums, different numbers. The same pillar has one latitude and longitude on WGS84 and different ones on the older Indian datum on the Everest ellipsoid, because the two ellipsoids differ in size, shape and position. The difference is large enough to put a point in the wrong plot or on the wrong side of a road, so coordinates are transformed to one datum before they are combined, with the transformation stated.

answer.text: Heights need a surface too. GNSS gives h above the ellipsoid; levelling gives H above the geoid. They differ by the geoid undulation N, which can be tens of metres.
answer.pre:
h = 52.3 m, N = −82.0 m   →   H = h − N = 134.3 m
using h as if it were H puts the point 82.0 m too low

answer: Projected coordinates need their zone. In UTM a point at 13.08° N, 80.27° E is in zone 44 (central meridian 81° E). Its easting is below the false easting of 500 000 m because it is 0.73° west of the central meridian. The same easting and northing quoted without "zone 44N" could be a point in any of the 60 zones.

Engineering consequences. Setting out: a building set out from GNSS coordinates on one datum and a drawing on another lands in the wrong place. Flood work: a flood level given above mean sea level but compared with GNSS heights is wrong by N. GIS: two layers on different datums do not overlay.
Good practice. Record with every coordinate set the datum, the projection and zone, the vertical datum (or the geoid model used), the units and the date of observation.

answer.text: Seconds into metres. One second of latitude is R × 4.848 × 10⁻⁶ = 30.9 m on the ground; one second of longitude at latitude 13° is 30.9 × cos 13° = 30.1 m. A datum difference of only a few seconds is therefore a shift of about a hundred metres.

answer: Decimal places matter too. 13.08° N, 80.27° E is given to 0.01°, so each value could be off by 0.005° = 0.005 × 111.3 km = 557 m. A position for setting out needs about seven decimal places of a degree (about 1 cm), and the datum, before the digits mean anything.

Example of a misfit. A pipeline drawing in a local datum and a contractor's GNSS on WGS84 can disagree by tens to hundreds of metres in position and by N in height; the pipe gradient worked from mixed heights can even reverse.
Check. Zone = whole part of (80.27 + 180)/6, plus 1 = 43 + 1 = 44; central meridian = 6 × 44 − 183 = 81°.

bank.q: Assess the sources of error in an EDM observation and suggest practical steps to keep a total station traverse within 1 in 10000 closing accuracy.
outline: Instrument errors: zero error, scale error, prism constant, phase resolution.
Atmospheric errors: temperature and pressure affect wave speed; enter corrected values or let the instrument do it.
Pointing and centring errors, prism alignment, height of instrument and target.
Reflectorless measurement: weaker return, shorter range, larger error, careful on dark or inclined surfaces.
Practise: forced centring, measure each distance both ways, close the traverse, adjust by Bowditch or transit rule, apply curvature and refraction to long lines.
answer: Target. A closed traverse of six legs of 200 m has a perimeter of 1200 m. Closing to 1 in 10 000 allows a closing error of 1200/10 000 = 0.12 m.

answer.text: Random distance error. An EDM of ±(3 mm + 3 ppm) gives 3 + 3 × 0.2 = 3.6 mm on each leg; six independent legs together give about √6 × 3.6 mm.
answer.pre:
per leg:     3 + 3 × 0.200 = 3.6 mm
six legs:    √6 × 3.6 = 8.8 mm   (well inside 120 mm)

answer.text: Angle and centring errors. An angle error of 5″ at a station swings the next station sideways by 200 × 5/206 265 m; a centring error of 2 mm at each end adds a few millimetres more.
Instrument and atmosphere.

head: Source
Effect
Control
rows: enter the right constant; check on a baseline
measure at the instrument and enter
forced centring, tribrachs left in place

answer: What the closure cannot show. A wrong prism constant adds the same length to each leg, and a scale error stretches every leg in proportion. A closed polygon stretched or padded uniformly can still close (for a regular hexagon the six added 30 mm pieces point in six directions and cancel), so a traverse may close well while every coordinate is wrong. Only a calibrated baseline or a known distance between two control points reveals these errors.

Practical steps. Calibrate the EDM on a baseline before the job; enter the prism constant of the prism in use; measure temperature and pressure at the instrument at each station; use forced centring; measure each leg in both directions and compare; observe angles on both faces; avoid very short legs next to long ones; close on known control, and adjust the small remaining misclosure by the Bowditch or transit rule.

answer.text: A wrong prism constant, worked. A −30 mm prism used with 0 mm entered makes each 200 m leg 30 mm too long:
answer.pre:
each leg: 200/0.030 = 1 in 6 667 (fails 1 in 10 000 on every line)
perimeter: 6 × 0.030 = 0.180 m too long, yet the hexagon still closes

answer.text: Atmosphere, worked. Entering 25 °C when the air is 35 °C leaves about 10 ppm uncorrected:
answer.pre: 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 m = 2 mm per leg;   10 × 10⁻⁶ × 1200 m = 12 mm on the perimeter

answer.text: Angular closure. The interior angles of a hexagon must sum to (2 × 6 − 4) × 90° = 720°. A common allowance for a total station traverse is about 5″√n:
Error budget for the traverse.

head: Source
Size
Within 0.12 m?
rows: 180 mm of length, hidden by closure
no: shows only on a baseline

answer: Check. The random budget (about 9 mm from distances and about 5 mm per station from angles) is a small part of 120 mm, so a misclosure near 0.12 m points to a blunder or a systematic error, not to ordinary scatter.

glossary.def: The art and science of determining the relative positions of points on or near the earth's surface and representing them to a convenient scale on a map or plan.
Surveying in which the curvature of the earth is taken into account and computations are made on a reference ellipsoid.
A survey that establishes a network of points of known high accuracy to which all detail surveys are referred.
Surveying of water bodies to fix depths, shore lines and underwater features for navigation and dredging.
Surveying in which positions are fixed from observations of stars, giving latitude, longitude and azimuth independent of ground control.
The difference between a measured value and the true value of the quantity.
A small error of unpredictable sign and size, caused by imperfect observation, which is reduced by repeated measurement and averaging.
The difference between an observed value and its adjusted or most probable value.
A scaled, conventional representation of features of the ground seen from above on a horizontal plane.
The scale written as a ratio 1:M, where one unit on the map stands for M of the same units on the ground.
The constant vertical distance between two successive contour lines on a map.
Latitude, longitude and height that define a position on a stated reference surface.
Plane coordinates, such as easting and northing in UTM, obtained by mathematically projecting the ellipsoid onto a flat surface.
The set of parameters and formulas used to convert coordinates from one geodetic datum to another.
The average height of the sea surface over a long period, used as the zero for heights.
The height of the geoid above (or below) the reference ellipsoid at a place, symbol N, in metres.
The longest and most carefully measured line of a chain survey, from which the framework of the survey is built.
A line measured in the field only to verify that the plotted framework is correct.
An offset measured at 90 degrees to the survey line, usually with a cross staff or optical square.
The ruled notebook in which all field measurements and sketches are recorded at the time of survey.
An instrument that measures distance by transmitting an electromagnetic signal to a reflector or target and measuring phase or time of travel.
The frequency at which the carrier wave of an EDM is varied; it sets the unit of length used to resolve the phase difference.
A correction applied to EDM distances for the actual temperature and pressure, since the speed of light in air depends on both.
